name: Set-Valued Action Spaces in Reinforcement Learning
key_paper: Chen, W., Wang, Y., & Yuan, Y. (2013). Combinatorial Multi-Armed Bandit: General Framework and Applications. ICML 2013. Secondary: Lattimore, T., & Szepesvari, C. (2020). Bandit Algorithms (Cambridge University Press) — Chapter 22: Combinatorial Bandits. Also foundational: Cesa-Bianchi, N., & Lugosi, G. (2012). Combinatorial Bandits. Journal of Computer and System Sciences, 78(5), 1404-1422.
algorithm_description: Set-valued action spaces formalize the RL problem where the agent must select a subset S of size k from a ground set of N items at each decision step, rather than a single scalar action. The action space has combinatorial size C(N, k) — for N=50, k=7 this is ~99 million possible actions, making tabular methods infeasible. The formal framework distinguishes three sub-problems: (1) Combinatorial bandits — a one-step version where a subset is selected and a reward observed, without state transitions; the key variants are semi-bandit feedback (reward observed per selected item) vs. bandit feedback (reward observed for the whole set). (2) Top-k selection — a special case where the goal is to identify the k highest-expected-reward items, studied as a pure exploration problem with PAC-style sample complexity bounds. (3) Action space factorization — decomposing the joint subset selection into a product of simpler distributions, enabling tractable policy gradient methods. The unifying theoretical insight is that the expected reward of a subset decomposes under linearity assumptions (CMAB-T model), enabling efficient algorithms that avoid enumeration.
action_space_handling: Three principal approaches exist for representing and sampling from set-valued action spaces: (1) Flat enumeration — enumerate all C(N,k) subsets explicitly; exact but computationally infeasible for N > 20, k > 3. (2) Factored independent sampling — assign a score/logit to each item independently, then select the top-k or sample without replacement; tractable in O(N log k) but cannot model inter-item correlations within the subset. (3) Autoregressive factorization — model the joint probability of a subset as a product of conditionals: P(S) = P(s1) * P(s2 | s1) * ... * P(sk | s1,...,s_{k-1}); expressive but requires k sequential forward passes and k-fold credit assignment. The combinatorial bandit literature primarily uses the factored independent model (items are assumed to be independent given context), while deep RL approaches increasingly use autoregressive factorization (pointer networks, transformer decoders) to capture within-subset correlations.
how_combinatorial_output_is_formed: The canonical mechanisms for generating a k-subset from {1..N} are: (1) Score-and-select (greedy top-k) — a network produces N scores, and the top-k by score are taken deterministically; non-differentiable, used in inference. (2) Gumbel-top-k sampling — add i.i.d. Gumbel noise to N logits and take top-k; produces an exact sample from the Plackett-Luce distribution without replacement; differentiable via soft-top-k relaxation. (3) Autoregressive masking — a recurrent or transformer decoder selects items one at a time, masking previously selected items; pointer networks (Vinyals et al. 2015) are the canonical architecture. (4) Determinantal Point Processes (DPPs) — a probabilistic model where P(S) is proportional to det(L_S) for a kernel matrix L; naturally models negative correlations (diversity) within the selected subset; sampling is O(Nk^2). (5) Action set embedding — embed each candidate subset (or a factored representation of it) and train a critic/Q-function on subset embeddings; avoids enumeration but requires generalization across exponentially many subsets.
sequential_generation_strategy: The literature identifies three generation strategies with distinct tradeoffs: (1) Joint (flat) — all k items are selected simultaneously from N independent logits using top-k or Gumbel-top-k; O(N) computation per play; cannot model within-subset correlations; probability model is Plackett-Luce (or Bernoulli multi-hot with post-hoc k-constraint); standard for combinatorial bandits. (2) Autoregressive — items are generated sequentially, each conditioned on previously selected items via masking or embedding; k forward passes required; captures co-occurrence structure; pointer networks and set transformers use this strategy; dominant in combinatorial optimization RL literature. (3) Energy/flow-based — a global energy function over subsets is defined and subsets are sampled via MCMC or a learned flow (GFlowNets); exact modeling of full joint distribution over subsets at cost of O(Nk) or O(N^2) computation; GFlowNets are the leading 2023-2024 representative of this approach for combinatorial generation tasks.
gradient_estimator_type: Several gradient estimators are applicable to set-valued action spaces, ordered by variance and bias: (1) REINFORCE (score function / likelihood-ratio) — applicable to any differentiable policy, unbiased but high variance; variance grows with k (k independent log-probability terms each contributing noise). (2) RLOO (Leave-One-Out baseline) — a per-sample baseline using other samples in the batch; reduces REINFORCE variance by a factor of (B-1)/B for batch size B; recommended for combinatorial outputs with small datasets. (3) Gumbel reparameterization — for Plackett-Luce / Gumbel-top-k policies; low variance reparameterization gradient; requires differentiable reward or surrogate. (4) Straight-through estimator — applied to hard top-k; high bias, low variance; common for binary subset selection when differentiability is needed cheaply. (5) Stochastic perturbation (SPSA / ES) — black-box gradient estimation via N-point perturbation; applicable when reward is non-differentiable; scales poorly with N. For the combinatorial bandit setting specifically, the semi-bandit gradient (CUCB, CombLinUCB) avoids gradient estimation entirely by using upper confidence bounds on per-item expected rewards.
combinatorial_constraint_enforcement: The formally studied mechanisms for enforcing exactly k distinct items from {1..N} are: (1) Hard top-k (argmax-based) — exactly k distinct items are selected by construction; non-differentiable; no chance of duplicates; standard in combinatorial bandit algorithms. (2) Without-replacement sampling (Gumbel-top-k, Plackett-Luce) — probabilistic selection of exactly k distinct items; differentiable via soft relaxation; no post-hoc filtering needed. (3) Autoregressive masking — at each of k steps, previously selected items have their logits set to -inf before softmax; exactly k distinct items by construction; differentiable through each step. (4) Constrained decoding with feasibility oracle — a general approach using Lagrangian relaxation or projection to enforce subset constraints; applicable to arbitrary combinatorial constraints beyond simple size k. (5) Post-hoc rejection sampling — sample with replacement then reject duplicates; simple but introduces bias, especially when k/N is large (e.g., k=7, N=50 means 14% of the pool selected, making duplicate collisions common). Theoretical analysis shows autoregressive masking is the only approach that simultaneously guarantees exact k, is differentiable, and can model correlations.
sample_efficiency_rating: medium-to-high for combinatorial bandits (with semi-bandit feedback); low for full combinatorial RL. Combinatorial bandit algorithms (CUCB, CombLinUCB, Thompson sampling for linear payoffs) achieve regret bounds of O(k * sqrt(N * T)) under the linear payoff assumption — this scales favorably because only N parameters (one per item) are estimated rather than C(N,k). With semi-bandit feedback (reward observed per selected item), each draw yields up to k signal observations rather than 1, giving a k-fold effective sample size improvement. Concretely: with N=50 items, k=7, and 100 historical draws, semi-bandit feedback yields up to 700 item-level reward observations — sufficient for Thompson sampling on per-item Bernoulli distributions to converge to reasonable posteriors. This is the strongest theoretical argument for using the combinatorial bandit framework over deep RL for this application. Full combinatorial RL (with state transitions and a learned policy network) loses this favorable scaling and reverts to standard RL sample complexity.
regularization_built_in: Regularization in set-valued action space methods varies by approach: (1) Combinatorial bandits (CUCB, Thompson sampling) — UCB confidence bounds and Thompson posterior widths act as implicit regularization; no overfitting in the traditional sense since these are non-parametric models. (2) Plackett-Luce policy gradient — entropy of the Plackett-Luce distribution over k-subsets can be computed in closed form and added as a bonus; the Gumbel temperature acts as an inverse regularization parameter (higher temperature = more entropic policy). (3) Autoregressive policies (pointer networks) — standard neural network regularization applies (dropout, weight decay, label smoothing on the sequential selections); additionally, the masking constraint prevents policy from converging to degenerate subsets with repeated items. (4) DPP-based selection — the determinant kernel in DPPs provides built-in diversity regularization (high probability subsets are those with maximally diverse items), which can be interpreted as a structural inductive bias against mode collapse. (5) Linear combinatorial bandits (CombLinUCB) — L2 regularization on the feature weight vector (ridge regression) is standard; provides generalization across items sharing features.
known_failure_modes_on_small_data: Documented failure modes for set-valued action spaces with n < 200: (1) Non-linear payoff violation — combinatorial bandit algorithms (CUCB, CombLinUCB) assume the expected reward of a subset decomposes as a sum/function of per-item rewards; lottery payoffs are highly non-linear (jackpot requires matching all k), and this assumption fails badly, causing theoretical guarantees to collapse. (2) Curse of combinations — methods that attempt to learn over the full subset space (Q-learning on subsets, value-based RL) face C(N,k) states and cannot generalize with n < 200 samples; any method using a lookup table over subsets will completely overfit. (3) Semi-bandit feedback mismatch — in a standard lottery draw, feedback is semi-bandit (we know which of our selected numbers matched) but the underlying ball distribution does not change between draws; some algorithms assume an adversarial or stochastic bandit model that does not match the lottery's fixed but unknown draw distribution. (4) Mode collapse in autoregressive policies — with sparse reward and fewer than 200 episodes, autoregressive policies (pointer networks) frequently collapse to outputting the same k-subset repeatedly; entropy regularization is insufficient without enough reward signal. (5) Overconfident posterior in Thompson sampling — with only 100 draws, the Beta/Dirichlet posterior over ball frequencies is heavily influenced by the prior choice; a flat (uninformative) prior can lead to either too-confident estimates early or too-diffuse estimates never converging.

data_regime_evidence.minimum_training_samples_tested: Combinatorial bandit papers (Chen et al. 2013, CUCB) prove regret bounds that hold for any T but do not specify a minimum T for the algorithm to outperform random selection. Empirically, CombLinUCB with semi-bandit feedback on N=50 items has been validated in recommendation system experiments with as few as 50-200 rounds (equivalent to draws) when items have rich feature representations (Qin et al. 2014, Cascading Bandits). Without features (pure bandit, Bernoulli rewards per item), the minimum T for meaningful convergence in N=50 is approximately 200-500 rounds per simulation study. For deep RL methods (pointer networks, set transformer + PPO), no published result demonstrates effective learning with fewer than 1000 training episodes on combinatorial tasks. The lottery-nn scenario (100-200 draws, no item features beyond historical frequency) falls at the boundary of the favorable regime for combinatorial bandits and entirely outside the validated regime for deep combinatorial RL.
data_regime_evidence.performance_degradation_curve: [uncertain] — No published degradation curve exists for combinatorial bandit or combinatorial RL methods specifically in the 50-200 sample range with lottery-like sparse, non-linear payoffs. The general bandit theory predicts O(k * sqrt(N * T)) cumulative regret, which improves monotonically with T; at T=100, N=50, k=7 this gives regret ~O(470) relative to the optimal policy — dominated by noise in the small-T regime. Empirical curves for CUCB and Thompson sampling on recommendation tasks with N=50, k=5 show convergence to near-optimal selection around T=300-500 rounds under Bernoulli reward assumptions.
data_regime_evidence.comparison_baseline: Chen et al. 2013 compare CUCB to UCB1 (single-item bandit ignoring combinatorial structure) and random selection; CUCB achieves lower regret per item-observation under the linear payoff model. Qin et al. 2014 (Cascading Bandits) show combinatorial UCB variants match or exceed greedy heuristics at T=200-500 on click-through-rate data (N=50, k=5). No paper directly compares combinatorial bandit vs. combinatorial RL in the n<200 regime; this gap in the literature is a known limitation acknowledged in recent survey papers (Lattimore & Szepesvari 2020, Chapter 22).

convergence_guarantees_small_n: Combinatorial bandit algorithms have the strongest formal guarantees of any set-valued action space method: (1) CUCB (Chen et al. 2013): O(k * sqrt(N * T * log T)) regret bound under the CMAB-T model (linear payoffs, semi-bandit feedback); finite-sample, not just asymptotic. (2) CombLinUCB (Wen et al. 2015): O(k * d * sqrt(T * log T)) regret where d is the feature dimension; stronger when items have informative features. (3) Thompson sampling for combinatorial bandits (Wang & Chen 2018): achieves Bayes-optimal regret under Beta-Bernoulli model with semi-bandit feedback; finite-sample posterior concentration holds for T > O(N log N / delta) with probability 1 - delta. (4) Pure exploration (top-k identification): PAC bounds give that O(N/epsilon^2 * log(N/delta)) samples are sufficient to identify the k best items with probability 1-delta (Bubeck et al. 2013); for N=50, epsilon=0.05, delta=0.05, this is ~12,000 samples — far beyond the lottery dataset. (5) Deep combinatorial RL: no finite-sample guarantees; asymptotic convergence under standard regularity conditions only. The key limitation: all combinatorial bandit guarantees assume the linear payoff model (CMAB-T), which is violated by lottery jackpot structure. [uncertain for non-linear payoff regime]
reward_distribution_handling: Set-valued action space theory addresses sparse and skewed rewards differently across its sub-frameworks: (1) Combinatorial bandits — designed for repeated selection with observed reward; handle sparse rewards by construction (UCB exploration ensures all items are tried; low-reward items are deprioritized, not ignored). However, jackpot-only rewards (binary win/loss) with p ~ 1e-7 are effectively never observed in 100 draws, making the bandit framework degenerate. Semi-bandit feedback (per-ball hit/miss) with reward = number_of_hits is the only practically viable reward signal — this transforms the problem from jackpot prediction to frequency/hot-number learning. (2) Deep combinatorial RL — reward shaping is essential; raw binary reward (jackpot won?) provides zero gradient signal. Shaped rewards (hit_count / k, or marginal gain per matched number) make the problem tractable at the cost of incentive misalignment. (3) Distributional approaches — distributional RL (IQN, C51) can model the full distribution of set-level rewards rather than just the expectation; this is theoretically attractive for lottery where the reward distribution is highly multimodal (nearly always 0, sometimes 1-7). Minimum draws for stable combinatorial RL: 500+ for semi-bandit feedback; effectively infinite for jackpot-only binary feedback without reward shaping.
credit_assignment_granularity: This is the theoretically most important field for the lottery application. Set-valued action space theory distinguishes: (1) Full-bandit feedback — only the total reward for the selected subset is observed; gradient signal is a single scalar per draw; hardest credit assignment problem; sample complexity O(C(N,k)) in worst case. (2) Semi-bandit feedback — the reward for each selected item is observed individually (for lottery: which numbers matched); reduces sample complexity from O(C(N,k)) to O(N) because per-item estimates can be maintained; enables combinatorial UCB and Thompson sampling algorithms with provable O(sqrt(NT)) regret vs. O(sqrt(C(N,k)*T)) for full-bandit. (3) Cascading feedback — a special semi-bandit variant where items are examined sequentially until one fails; not applicable to lottery. (4) Number-level credit in deep RL — when using policy gradient on a factored (independent) policy, the gradient for each item's logit is proportional to whether that item was selected times the total reward; this achieves number-level credit assignment implicitly when the policy is factored. True number-level credit (directly measuring item i's marginal contribution to subset reward) requires a Shapley value computation or a separate critic per item. For lottery-nn: using hit_count as reward with semi-bandit feedback (was ball i selected AND did it appear in the draw?) provides number-level credit and is the single most important design decision for sample efficiency.
diversity_mechanism: Diversity in set-valued action spaces is both a practical concern (generating different plays) and a formal optimality requirement in some frameworks: (1) Determinantal Point Processes (DPPs) — formally model repulsion between selected items via the determinant kernel; high-probability subsets are maximally diverse by mathematical construction; used in recommendation systems and summarization for explicit diversity. (2) Plackett-Luce / Gumbel-top-k — diversity arises from stochastic Gumbel perturbation; independent perturbations across items mean different plays are generated at each forward pass without explicit diversity reward; the temperature parameter controls entropy. (3) Submodular reward shaping — adding a submodular diversity penalty (e.g., coverage reward) to the bandit reward encourages exploration of different k-subsets; studied in combinatorial bandit literature for coverage objectives. (4) Population-based methods — maintaining a population of diverse policies (evolutionary strategies, Quality-Diversity algorithms) that collectively cover different regions of the subset space. (5) Entropy regularization — maximizing H(pi) over the distribution of k-subsets; for Plackett-Luce this is tractable; for autoregressive models this requires summing over all k sequential steps. For lottery-nn: Gumbel-top-k stochastic sampling provides sufficient diversity for generating distinct plays; DPPs provide structural diversity (selecting historically uncorrelated balls); entropy bonus prevents collapse to a single dominant play.
offline_vs_online_rl_compatibility: This is the critical axis for the lottery application (one real draw per week). Analysis by sub-framework: (1) Combinatorial bandits — inherently online (each UCB update requires a new observed reward); can be adapted for offline by treating historical draws as a fixed dataset and computing posterior estimates (Thompson sampling with Beta priors over ball frequencies); this is valid and efficient — each historical draw contributes k semi-bandit observations; fully offline operation is possible and theoretically grounded. (2) Linear combinatorial bandits (CombLinUCB) — offline training is straightforward: fit a ridge regression on historical (context, reward) pairs, then apply UCB exploration strategy; this is the standard offline contextual bandit approach. (3) Deep combinatorial RL — fundamentally online; offline adaptation requires importance weighting (per-decision importance sampling for factored policies), offline RL techniques (CQL, IQL), or behavior cloning pre-training; all add implementation complexity. (4) Top-k identification — a pure exploration problem; offline data from historical draws can directly inform which k balls have highest historical frequency; this is statistically valid (maximum likelihood estimate of ball probabilities from historical draws). Verdict: combinatorial bandit approaches (Thompson sampling, CombLinUCB) are fully compatible with offline training on historical draws; deep combinatorial RL requires explicit offline RL adaptation to work without online interaction.
key_dependencies: For combinatorial bandit approaches: NumPy/SciPy only (Thompson sampling is 20 lines of numpy; CombLinUCB requires ridge regression from scipy.linalg). For DPP-based methods: dppy library (pip install dppy) for efficient k-DPP sampling; alternatively torch-based DPP implementations. For action space factorization in deep RL: PyTorch only (factored Bernoulli heads or autoregressive transformer decoder). For Plackett-Luce / Gumbel-top-k: PyTorch only (no external dependency). For full combinatorial RL: torchrl (Meta's RL library) provides CompositeActionSpec for structured action spaces. Existing bandit.py in lottery-nn is the natural integration point — Thompson sampling for combinatorial bandits extends it with ~80 lines of additional code.
estimated_lines_of_code: 60-150 lines depending on chosen sub-method: (a) Thompson sampling combinatorial bandit with semi-bandit feedback: ~60-80 lines — extend existing bandit.py with per-ball Beta posteriors, k-subset selection via posterior sampling, and semi-bandit reward update; (b) CombLinUCB with ball feature vectors: ~100-120 lines — ridge regression fit, UCB score computation, greedy top-k selection; (c) Factored independent policy with Gumbel-top-k (deep RL): ~50-80 additional lines over existing predict.py — replace temperature-softmax sampling with Gumbel-top-k primitive; (d) Full autoregressive policy with masking: ~200-300 lines — new decoder module, sequential masking loop, k-step advantage estimation; (e) DPP-based diverse subset sampling: ~80-100 lines — kernel matrix construction from ball logits, k-DPP sampling call via dppy.
transfer_learning_compatibility: Excellent for all deep learning sub-methods. The existing SharedLotteryTransformer produces per-ball logits (main_logits: [batch, N]) which are exactly the input required by Gumbel-top-k, autoregressive masking, or factored Bernoulli policies. No architectural changes to the backbone are required. For combinatorial bandit methods (Thompson sampling, CombLinUCB), transfer is indirect: the transformer's logits can serve as informative priors for the bandit's per-ball score estimates, or the backbone can be frozen and only the bandit posterior maintained on top. This hybrid (pretrained neural backbone + combinatorial bandit on top of its outputs) is the most practical and transfer-compatible integration pattern for the lottery-nn project, combining the backbone's sequence modeling capability with the bandit's theoretical sample-efficiency guarantees.
specific_application_in_project: Set-valued action space theory provides the formal foundation for the entire Phase 2 Actor-Critic play generation system and the existing bandit.py. Concrete applications: (1) Theoretical justification for Thompson sampling in bandit.py — the existing Thompson sampling implementation is a combinatorial bandit with semi-bandit feedback; understanding the CMAB-T framework clarifies when its guarantees hold (linear payoff assumption: number of hits = sum of per-ball hit indicators) and when they break (jackpot-only reward). (2) Semi-bandit feedback implementation — the most impactful code change is converting the current play-level reward (hit_count) into per-ball semi-bandit rewards: for each play, record which of the k selected balls matched the draw; update each matched ball's Beta posterior separately. This is a 20-line change to bandit.py that provides a k-fold improvement in effective sample size. (3) Gumbel-top-k integration — replace the current rejection-sampling loop in predict.py with a Gumbel-top-k forward pass over the transformer's logits; this is Phase 2's core Actor mechanism, grounded in the Plackett-Luce theory of set-valued actions. (4) DPP diversity sampling — optionally replace naive entropy-temperature diversity with DPP-based selection of diverse plays from the posterior distribution, using historical ball co-occurrence as the diversity kernel. Applies to all three lotteries (LottoMax, 6/49, Daily Grand) since all share the same SharedLotteryTransformer backbone.
integration_point: Phase 2 (Actor-Critic play generation) + Bandit (extend bandit.py with semi-bandit feedback)
replaces_or_extends: Extends bandit.py with semi-bandit (per-ball) reward updates and combinatorial posterior sampling. Extends predict.py by grounding the current temperature-softmax sampling in Plackett-Luce theory and replacing the rejection-sampling duplicate-avoidance loop with Gumbel-top-k. Does not replace the SharedLotteryTransformer backbone.

benchmark_results: Key empirical results from the combinatorial bandit and set-valued RL literature: (1) CUCB (Chen et al. 2013, ICML): achieves O(k * sqrt(N*T*log T)) regret on synthetic combinatorial problems; outperforms naive UCB1 (treating each subset as an arm) by factor of C(N,k) / N in sample complexity. (2) CombLinUCB / LinUCB for slates (Qin et al. 2014): on Yahoo! news recommendation (N=271 articles, k=5 slots), semi-bandit LinUCB achieves CTR 6-8% above random selection within 200 rounds, comparable to full-bandit methods needing 1000+ rounds. (3) Cascading Bandits (Kveton et al. 2015, AISTATS): KL-UCB variant achieves near-optimal regret on click-through data with N=50, k=5 within 500 rounds. (4) DPP for diverse recommendation (Chen et al. 2018, KDD): DPP-based set selection improves diversity metrics by 30-50% vs. greedy top-k while maintaining >90% of relevance score. (5) Pointer networks for combinatorial RL (Bello et al. 2016, ICLR): REINFORCE-trained pointer network solves TSP-50 to within 1-2% of optimal using 1M training instances — not directly applicable to small-data regime. (6) No benchmark exists for any of these methods on lottery-specific tasks (N~50, k~7, sparse non-linear reward, n<200 draws).
notable_use_cases: Structurally similar real-world applications of set-valued action space methods: (1) Slate recommendation systems — Netflix, YouTube, and Spotify select k=5-20 items from N=10k-1M candidates; semi-bandit feedback (user clicks on individual items) enables efficient combinatorial bandit learning; this is the closest structural analog to lottery play generation at the algorithm level, though N and T are much larger. (2) Clinical trial arm selection — selecting k treatment combinations from N possible interventions; small sample sizes (n<200 patients), non-linear (interaction) payoffs, semi-bandit feedback (per-treatment outcome observed); the non-linear payoff challenge matches the lottery jackpot structure. (3) Portfolio optimization — selecting k assets from N candidates to maximize risk-adjusted return; subset constraints (budget, sector limits), sparse reward (annual return), and correlation structure between selected assets — structurally very close to lottery, studied under submodular maximization and combinatorial bandit frameworks. (4) Drug combination screening — selecting k compounds from N candidates; combinatorial synergy effects, expensive reward observations (~cost-per-experiment analogous to cost-per-draw), small dataset regime; active area connecting combinatorial bandits to Bayesian optimization. (5) Feature subset selection in AutoML — selecting k features from N to maximize validation accuracy; offline dataset, combinatorial structure; Thompson sampling and greedy submodular approaches are standard.
